concepts.title: application.properties, application.yml, and Property Precedence
concepts.description: Spring Boot reads configuration from a strict, ordered set of sources -- command-line arguments, environment variables, profile-specific files, application.properties/yml, and more -- merging them into one unified Environment, and knowing that precedence order is exactly what lets you predict which value actually wins when the same property is set in more than one place.
learningObjectives: Write equivalent configuration in application.properties and application.yml and explain the structural difference between flat dot-notation keys and nested YAML mappings.
Explain what the Environment abstraction is and how it presents multiple underlying property sources as one queryable view.
List the most commonly encountered property sources in their relative order of precedence.
Predict which value wins when the same property is set in both application.properties and as a command-line argument.
Explain why YAML's indentation sensitivity is a common source of silent misconfiguration compared to the flatter .properties format.
Explain relaxed binding and why an environment variable like ORDER_SERVICE_URL can satisfy a property key named order-service.url.

sections.heading: Two File Formats, One Underlying Model
sections.body:
`application.properties` represents configuration as flat, dot-notation key-value pairs, one per line:

```properties
server.port=8081
spring.datasource.url=jdbc:postgresql://localhost:5432/orders
spring.datasource.username=orders_app
app.notifications.retry-count=3
```

`application.yml` represents the same information as a nested mapping, where indentation encodes the hierarchy that `.properties` spells out with dots:

```yaml
server:
  port: 8081
spring:
  datasource:
    url: jdbc:postgresql://localhost:5432/orders
    username: orders_app
app:
  notifications:
    retry-count: 3
```

Both are read from the same place by default (typically `src/main/resources`), both flow into the same underlying configuration model once parsed, and Spring Boot supports either one, but if both `application.properties` and `application.yml` are present in the same location at once, `.properties` takes precedence for any key they both define, so pick one format per project. YAML avoids repeating a long common prefix on every line of deeply nested configuration, but that nesting is also its main hazard: indentation is *significant*. Two spaces too few often isn't a parse error; the key moves under a different parent, so the property binds to the wrong place, or nowhere, with no warning.

sections.heading: The Environment Abstraction: One Queryable View Over Many Sources
sections.body: Every configuration source (the properties file, environment variables, command-line arguments, and several others) is registered as a `PropertySource` inside a single `Environment` object, and every mechanism that reads configuration (`@Value`, `@ConfigurationProperties`, and every autoconfiguration class discussed in the Core Concepts module) reads through that one `Environment`, never directly from a file. Calling `environment.getProperty("server.port")` walks the ordered list of registered `PropertySource`s and returns the value from the *first* one that defines that key. That is how precedence works: lower-priority sources are not ignored or merged in, the search just stops at the first match. A component reading `spring.datasource.url` never needs to know whether the value came from a file, an environment variable, or a command-line flag. From its point of view there is one `Environment`, with one value for that key.

sections.heading: Precedence Order: What Wins When Two Sources Disagree
sections.body:
Spring Boot's documented precedence list has over a dozen source types (devtools settings, `@TestPropertySource`, and more). The ones you will meet daily, from highest to lowest precedence, are:

1. Command-line arguments (`--server.port=9090`)
2. Java System properties (`-Dserver.port=9090`), then OS environment variables (`SERVER_PORT=9090`)
3. Profile-specific files, `application-{profile}.properties`/`.yml` (covered fully in the Profiles concept later in this module)
4. The base `application.properties`/`.yml`
5. `@PropertySource`-referenced files and any hardcoded defaults in `@ConfigurationProperties` classes

Sources further up are more specific to a particular deployment or run; sources further down are more generic and baked into the build. A value in `application.properties` is the sensible default for the application in general; an argument or environment variable supplied when a container starts says what this instance needs right now, and it should win without anyone repackaging anything.

One refinement to points 3 and 4: files *outside* the jar (for example in a `config/` directory next to it) rank above files packaged *inside* it, even profile-specific ones. An external `application.properties` therefore beats a packaged `application-prod.properties`, which surprises people who expect profile files to win always. When a value is not what you expect, `/actuator/env` (if Actuator is on the classpath and the endpoint is exposed) lists every property source with the value each one holds for a key.

sections.heading: Relaxed Binding: Why Environment Variables Don't Need to Match the Property Key Exactly
sections.body:
A property key like `order-service.url` is normal in `application.properties`, but POSIX shells don't allow dots or hyphens in variable names you `export`. Spring Boot solves this with **relaxed binding**: it maps environment variable names onto property keys, with uppercase for lowercase and underscores for dots. An environment variable named `ORDER_SERVICE_URL` therefore satisfies the property key `order-service.url` with no mapping code.

The documented conversion is: replace dots with underscores, *remove* hyphens, uppercase, giving `ORDERSERVICE_URL`. The form with underscores in place of hyphens, used in this lesson, is also accepted and is what most deployments use. Write keys in kebab-case inside `@Value("${order-service.url}")` too; a camelCase key there does not match the other spellings. The restriction on dots and hyphens applies to environment variables only: a JVM system property such as `-Dorder-service.url=...` can use the property key as written.

Deployment tooling (Docker, Kubernetes manifests, CI/CD pipelines) mostly passes configuration through environment variables in `UPPER_SNAKE_CASE`. Relaxed binding lets an ops team override `order-service.url` that way, while the code and properties file keep kebab-case.

examples.title: The Same Configuration in .properties and .yml
examples.code:
# application.properties
server.port=8081
spring.datasource.url=jdbc:postgresql://localhost:5432/orders
spring.datasource.username=orders_app
app.notifications.retry-count=3

# ---
# application.yml (equivalent, nested instead of dot-separated)
# server:
#   port: 8081
# spring:
#   datasource:
#     url: jdbc:postgresql://localhost:5432/orders
#     username: orders_app
# app:
#   notifications:
#     retry-count: 3
examples.explanation: Every dot in the .properties keys corresponds to one level of nesting in the .yml version: spring.datasource.url becomes spring: / datasource: / url: three levels deep. Both formats produce the same set of resolved key-value pairs once Spring Boot parses them into the Environment; @ConfigurationProperties classes and @Value placeholders see no difference. The tradeoff is readability against risk: .yml avoids repeating spring.datasource. on every line once you have many keys under one prefix, at the cost of every line's meaning depending on how many spaces of indentation it has.

examples.title: Command-Line Arguments Overriding a File-Based Default
examples.code:
# application.properties, committed to the repository
server.port=8080

# Deployment / local override, with no code or file changes:
# java -jar app.jar --server.port=9090
#
# Application actually starts listening on port 9090, not 8080.
examples.explanation: server.port=8080 in application.properties establishes the generic default baked into the build. Passing --server.port=9090 as a command-line argument registers a PropertySource with higher precedence than the properties file. The Environment resolves a key by returning the value from the first source that defines it, so it finds 9090 and never reaches the file's 8080. The file is not edited or deleted; its value is shadowed for as long as the argument is supplied. That is how the identical jar runs on 8080 in one environment and 9090 in another with no rebuild.

examples.title: Relaxed Binding: An Environment Variable Satisfying a Kebab-Case Property
examples.code:
# application.properties
order-service.url=http://localhost:8082

# Container environment variable (typical Docker/Kubernetes style):
# ORDER_SERVICE_URL=https://orders.internal.example.com
#
# A component reading order-service.url via @Value or @ConfigurationProperties
# resolves to https://orders.internal.example.com when this env var is present --
# no explicit mapping between the two names was written anywhere.
examples.explanation: Spring Boot's relaxed binding treats ORDER_SERVICE_URL as another spelling of order-service.url. Because environment variables rank above application.properties, setting it in a container overrides the file's value when that container starts, with no change to the jar or the file. Watch for accidental matches too: a variable some other tool sets, such as one Kubernetes injects for a service with the same name, can override your file with nothing in the repository to show it.

misconceptions.description: If a property is set in application.properties, that's the final, authoritative value -- command-line arguments or environment variables are only useful for setting values that AREN'T already in the file.
misconceptions.clarification: application.properties sits relatively low in Spring Boot's precedence order, so that more deployment-specific sources (command-line arguments, environment variables, profile-specific files) can override it. A property defined in BOTH the file and a higher-precedence source doesn't cause a conflict or an error; the higher-precedence source's value wins, with the file's value never being read for that key on that particular run. The file holds the default for the application in general, and the sources above it say what this particular run needs. That is what lets one built artifact behave differently across environments (different database URLs, ports, feature flags) without anyone editing the file.
misconceptions.fact: application.properties sits relatively low in Spring Boot's precedence order, specifically so that more deployment-specific sources -- command-line arguments, environment variables, profile-specific files -- can override it.

misconceptions.description: YAML and .properties are just two interchangeable syntaxes for writing the exact same file -- indentation in YAML is a style preference, similar to code formatting, not something that changes the file's meaning.
misconceptions.clarification: YAML's indentation is significant, not cosmetic. It's how the format encodes nesting, since there are no dots to do that job as there are in .properties. Shifting a key one space to the left or right can move it to a different level of nesting. Often the result is still valid YAML, so there is no parse error, just a value that binds under the wrong parent, or under no meaningful parent, and is never applied. That is harder to notice than a mistyped key in a flat .properties file, where every line carries its full path.

exercises.prompt: Given an application.properties file containing `server.port=8080`, the application is started with the command `java -jar app.jar --server.port=9090`. What port does the embedded server actually listen on, and why?
exercises.code:
# application.properties
server.port=8080

# Startup command:
# java -jar app.jar --server.port=9090
hints: Command-line arguments and application.properties are two separate PropertySources inside the same Environment -- which one has higher precedence?
The Environment resolves a key by returning the value from the FIRST source, in precedence order, that defines it -- it doesn't merge or average conflicting values.
Nothing about the file itself changes; the file's value for server.port is simply never reached during resolution on this particular run.
exercises.expectedAnswer: 9090. Command-line arguments rank above application.properties in Spring Boot's property source precedence, so the Environment resolves server.port to the command-line value; application.properties's value of 8080 is shadowed for this run, not overwritten in the file itself.
exercises.solutionExplanation: Both the command-line argument and the properties file register a value for the same key, server.port, as two separate PropertySources inside the application's single Environment. Command-line arguments sit at the top of Spring Boot's precedence order, above application.properties, so when anything (in this case, the autoconfiguration responsible for the embedded server) asks the Environment for server.port, it returns the first value found while walking sources in precedence order, which is the command-line argument's 9090. The file is unchanged, and starting the same jar WITHOUT the argument goes back to 8080, which is how one build serves several environments.

exercises.prompt: A developer expects app.notifications.retry-count to be nested under app.notifications, but @ConfigurationProperties(prefix = "app.notifications") always reports retryCount as its default value of 1, never the 5 from this file. Find and fix the YAML indentation bug.
hints: Compare the indentation level of retry-count and channel against the indentation level of notifications directly above them.

In YAML, a key nests under whichever key directly above it has LESS indentation and ends with a colon -- retry-count and channel here are at the exact same indentation as notifications, not one level deeper.
Indent retry-count and channel two more spaces than notifications so they become children of it, rather than unrelated siblings at the same level as notifications itself.
exercises.solutionExplanation: In the buggy version, notifications: has no keys indented further than itself: retry-count and channel sit at the SAME indentation level as notifications, which YAML interprets as them being siblings of notifications under app, not children of it. That produces a property path of app.retry-count (not app.notifications.retry-count), which @ConfigurationProperties(prefix = "app.notifications") never looks at, so its retryCount field is left at whatever default was set in the Java class, 1, with no parsing error anywhere, since app.retry-count is itself valid YAML. Running with Actuator's /actuator/env endpoint, or printing the property, shows the key under its wrong path. Indenting retry-count and channel two spaces further than notifications makes them nest underneath it, producing the intended app.notifications.retry-count path that the @ConfigurationProperties class is configured to read from.

assessments.prompt: A property is defined in both an OS environment variable and application.properties, with different values. Which value does Spring Boot's Environment resolve to?
options: application.properties always wins, because it's explicitly part of the application's own packaged configuration, so it overrides anything set outside it.
Whichever source was read first at startup wins, which is effectively random.
Spring Boot throws a startup exception because the same property is defined in two conflicting places.
The environment variable's value wins, because OS environment variables rank above application.properties in Spring Boot's property source precedence order.
assessments.explanation: OS environment variables sit above application.properties in Spring Boot's precedence order because they represent deployment-time, environment-specific configuration meant to be able to override generic, build-time defaults, so the Environment resolves to the environment variable's value. The “application.properties always wins, because it's explicitly part…” option inverts the actual precedence. The “Spring Boot throws a startup exception…” option is wrong: having the same key defined in multiple sources is normal, because overriding is the intended use. The “Whichever source was read first at startup…” option is wrong: resolution follows a fixed, documented, deterministic precedence order, not source-read timing.

assessments.prompt: A project's src/main/resources directory accidentally contains both application.properties and application.yml, and both define a value for server.port, with different numbers. Which value does Spring Boot actually use?
options: Spring Boot refuses to start, treating the same key appearing in two different file formats as a fatal conflict.
application.properties's value wins, because when both files are present in the same location, .properties takes precedence over .yml for any key they both define.
application.yml's value wins, because YAML files are always evaluated after .properties files by convention.
Spring Boot merges the two values into a single comma-separated string.
assessments.explanation: When application.properties and application.yml are both present in the same location, .properties takes precedence for any key they both define, which is why mixing the two formats in one project is worth avoiding, since edits to the losing file have no effect for overlapping keys. The failure is quiet: someone edits application.yml, sees no change, and has no error to explain why. The “Spring Boot refuses to start, treating…” option invents a startup failure that doesn't occur. The “application.yml's value wins, because YAML files…” option reverses the actual precedence. The “Spring Boot merges the two values into…” option describes behavior Spring Boot does not have.

assessments.prompt: A property key is written as `app.feature-flags.new-checkout` in application.properties. Which of the following can you export from a POSIX shell as an environment variable and have Spring Boot recognize it, via relaxed binding, as that same key?
options: APP_FEATURE_FLAGS_NEW_CHECKOUT
APP.FEATURE-FLAGS.NEW-CHECKOUT, uppercased but keeping the original dots and hyphens
appFeatureFlagsNewCheckout, written in camelCase with no separators at all
app.feature-flags.new-checkout, set verbatim as the environment variable's literal name
assessments.explanation: Relaxed binding lets an UPPER_SNAKE_CASE variable satisfy a dotted, kebab-case property key. (Spring's documentation gives APP_FEATUREFLAGS_NEWCHECKOUT, with hyphens removed, as the canonical form; the version with underscores is accepted as well.) The “app.feature-flags.new-checkout, set verbatim as the environment variable's literal name” and “APP.FEATURE-FLAGS.NEW-CHECKOUT, uppercased but keeping the original dots and hyphens” options keep dots and/or hyphens, which a POSIX shell does not allow in an exported variable's name. The “appFeatureFlagsNewCheckout, written in camelCase with no separators at all” option uses camelCase with no word-boundary markers at all, so relaxed binding cannot tell where app, feature-flags and new-checkout begin.

assessments.prompt: spring.profiles.active=prod is set, and both application.properties and application-prod.properties define a value for app.max-connections, with different numbers. Which value does the Environment resolve to, and why?
options: Neither -- defining the same key in both the base file and a profile-specific file triggers a startup error.
Whichever file happens to load last during startup, which is effectively non-deterministic run to run.
application-prod.properties's value, because profile-specific files rank above the base application.properties in Spring Boot's property source precedence order.
application.properties's value, because the base file is always treated as authoritative regardless of which profile is active, and profile files can only add new keys.
assessments.explanation: Profile-specific files rank above the base application.properties/.yml (when both are packaged together) because a profile-specific file represents a more deployment-specific override than the generic, build-time default in the base file, so for a key both files define, the profile-specific file's value wins. Both files are still loaded; the profile file only wins for the keys it redefines. The “application.properties's value, because the base file…” option inverts this relationship. The “Whichever file happens to load last during…” option is wrong: resolution follows a fixed, deterministic order, not load timing. The “Neither -- defining the same key…” option is wrong: that overlap is how profile-specific overrides work.

assessments.prompt: A teammate maintains three separate copies of application.properties -- one per environment -- and manually swaps the right one into the build before each deployment. Explain, using the Environment and precedence concepts, a better approach that avoids maintaining multiple property files by hand.
assessments.modelAnswer: The core problem with maintaining three separate application.properties files is that it ties environment-specific values (database URLs, feature flags, ports) to which FILE gets built into the artifact, so the artifact differs per environment, and the files drift out of sync over time. The better approach uses the fact that Spring Boot's Environment merges many property sources into one queryable view with a defined precedence order. Instead of three files, you'd keep ONE application.properties containing only the values that are the same everywhere (or sensible generic defaults), and supply everything that's environment-specific (the database URL, an API key, a feature flag) through a higher-precedence source at deploy time: OS environment variables set in the container/orchestration platform, or command-line arguments passed to the same jar. Because environment variables and command-line arguments both rank above application.properties in the resolution order, the SAME built jar picks up different values for those keys based on what the deployment environment supplies at startup, so there is nothing to rebuild or swap and no second file to drift out of sync. Profile-specific overlay files, covered in a later concept in this module, are the next step when a handful of non-secret values differ per environment.

concepts.title: @Value vs @ConfigurationProperties
concepts.description: @Value pulls in one property at a time through a placeholder expression, while @ConfigurationProperties binds a whole group of related keys onto a strongly-typed, optionally validated class -- and picking the wrong one for a given job trades away either simplicity or the fail-fast safety that grouped, validated configuration classes give you almost for free.
learningObjectives: Inject a single scalar property with @Value, including the ${property.key:defaultValue} placeholder syntax.
Bind a group of related properties into a strongly-typed class using @ConfigurationProperties and a prefix.
Explain why an @ConfigurationProperties class needs to be registered as a bean via @Component, @EnableConfigurationProperties, or @ConfigurationPropertiesScan before binding actually happens.
Explain constructor binding for an immutable @ConfigurationProperties class and why it's preferred over mutable setter binding.
Explain why @ConfigurationProperties classes can be validated with @Validated and JSR-380 constraint annotations in a way plain @Value usage generally isn't.
Predict the difference in failure behavior between a typo'd property key used with @Value and one used with a validated @ConfigurationProperties class.

sections.heading: @Value: One Property at a Time, Inline
@ConfigurationProperties: Binding a Whole Group as One Object
Constructor Binding for Immutability
Validation and Fail-Fast Configuration

examples.title: @Value With and Without a Default
examples.explanation: retryCount has a default of 3, so a missing app.notifications.retry-count property resolves to that fallback, which suits a property with a sensible default. channel has none, which is the right choice for a property with no reasonable fallback: if it's missing everywhere, Spring throws during placeholder resolution rather than injecting null, so startup fails instead of leaving a NotificationClient whose channel is never set. The tradeoff is that this fail-fast behavior only applies to properties without a default. Add one to channel and a typo'd key would go unnoticed again, always falling back to that default.

examples.title: A Registered, Grouped @ConfigurationProperties Class
examples.explanation: @ConfigurationPropertiesScan on the main application class registers NotificationProperties as a bean. Without it (or @Component on the class, or @EnableConfigurationProperties elsewhere), NotificationService could not be created and startup would fail with a missing-bean error. If nothing injected the class there would be no error at all, and an instance created with `new` would keep its Java defaults of 3 and "email" regardless of what application.properties says. Once registered, NotificationService receives the fully-bound NotificationProperties bean through ordinary constructor injection, like any other dependency: grouping app.notifications.retry-count and app.notifications.channel behind one typed object, rather than two separate @Value fields scattered wherever they're individually needed.

examples.title: Constructor Binding With Validation, Failing Fast on Bad Config
examples.explanation: Because NotificationProperties has exactly one constructor, Spring Boot uses it automatically for constructor binding: both fields are final and populated in one construction step, with no mutable intermediate state. @Validated tells Spring Boot to run Bean Validation against the fully-bound object immediately after construction, checking channel against @NotBlank and retryCount against @Min(0). With the shown (invalid) configuration, both constraints fail, and the application refuses to start, printing which properties failed, their values, and why. A bad deployment is caught when the container boots, not as a mysterious failure the first time some code path uses an empty channel or a negative retry count.

misconceptions.description: @Value("${some.key:default}") is just as safe as a strongly-typed, validated @ConfigurationProperties class -- if the real property key is ever typo'd elsewhere in configuration, at least there's a default, so nothing actually breaks.
misconceptions.clarification: That silent fallback is the danger, not a safety net. With a default, a typo'd key produces no error, no warning and no visible signal that the intended override was never applied: the application looks healthy while running with the wrong configuration indefinitely. In a validated @ConfigurationProperties class, leave required fields without a default and constrain them (@NotBlank, @Min, etc.), and a missing or invalid value stops startup. A default value in the class itself would reintroduce the same blind spot. Grouping keys under one prefix also makes a stray or misplaced key easier to spot in review.

misconceptions.description: Any class annotated @ConfigurationProperties is automatically registered as a bean and starts binding configuration immediately, the same way @Component works.
misconceptions.clarification: @ConfigurationProperties by itself is only metadata describing what prefix a class should bind to and how. It is not a stereotype annotation, and it does not, on its own, make Spring register the class as a bean. The class still needs to become a bean through some other mechanism: @Component on the class itself (if it's otherwise reachable by component scanning), @EnableConfigurationProperties(SomeProperties.class) declared on a @Configuration class, or @ConfigurationPropertiesScan on the main application class. Skip all three and nothing binds it: injecting it fails startup with a missing-bean error, while an instance you create yourself with new only has its Java defaults.
misconceptions.fact: @ConfigurationProperties by itself is only metadata describing what prefix a class should bind to and how -- it is not a stereotype annotation, and it does not, on its own, make Spring register the class as a bean.

exercises.prompt: A developer sets app.payment.provider=stripe and app.payment.timeout-seconds=10 in application.properties, but the application fails to start: "Parameter 0 of constructor in PaymentService required a bean of type 'PaymentProperties' that could not be found." Component scanning covers both classes' package. Find and fix the bug.
hints: @ConfigurationProperties alone only describes HOW a class should bind, if it ever becomes a bean at all -- is PaymentProperties actually registered as a bean anywhere here?
Compare this to @Component: without some registration mechanism, does Spring Data JPA-style automatic discovery apply to @ConfigurationProperties the same way?

Add @Component to the class, or @EnableConfigurationProperties(PaymentProperties.class) on a @Configuration class, or @ConfigurationPropertiesScan on the main application class -- any one of the three fixes this.
exercises.solutionExplanation: PaymentProperties was never registered as a Spring bean at all: @ConfigurationProperties only describes the prefix and binding shape for a class IF that class becomes a bean through some other mechanism, and none was present here, so PaymentService's constructor argument could not be satisfied. (Creating the object with new to get past the error would start the app, but with the unbound defaults "none" and 5.) Adding @Component makes PaymentProperties discoverable by ordinary component scanning, which registers it as a bean; once it IS a bean, Spring Boot's configuration-properties binding machinery runs against it, reading app.payment.provider and app.payment.timeout-seconds from the Environment and overwriting the Java defaults with the real configured values. @EnableConfigurationProperties(PaymentProperties.class) on a @Configuration class, or @ConfigurationPropertiesScan on the main application class, would each fix it too; those two are the better choice when you later move to constructor binding.

exercises.prompt: Given this class and these two application.properties scenarios, what happens when the application starts in each case?
hints: Notice there is no default value supplied in the ${...} placeholder -- what does @Value do when the property is missing and the placeholder has no default to fall back on?
In Scenario A, the property exists somewhere in the Environment -- resolution succeeds normally.
In Scenario B, the Environment has no value at all for app.reports.cron-expression, and there's no colon-separated default in the placeholder to fall back on.
exercises.expectedAnswer: Scenario A starts normally, with cronExpression bound to '0 0 * * * *'. Scenario B fails to start with IllegalArgumentException: Could not resolve placeholder 'app.reports.cron-expression', because the property has no value anywhere in the Environment and the @Value expression supplies no default to fall back on.
exercises.solutionExplanation: The placeholder ${app.reports.cron-expression} has no colon-separated default value written into it, which means Spring has no fallback to use if the real property is missing. In Scenario A, app.reports.cron-expression is defined in application.properties, so the Environment resolves it successfully and ReportScheduler is constructed normally with cronExpression set to the configured cron string. In Scenario B, no property source defines that key at all, and because there's no default to fall back to, Spring's placeholder resolution throws IllegalArgumentException while trying to construct ReportScheduler, which fails the entire application startup rather than silently leaving cronExpression as null. Adding a default (e.g., :0 0 * * * *) would turn Scenario B into a normal start using that default.

assessments.prompt: A team has six related properties, all under the prefix app.email.*, currently injected individually with six separate @Value fields scattered across three different classes. What is the most accurate reason to consolidate them into one @ConfigurationProperties class instead?
options: @ConfigurationProperties resolves properties faster at runtime than @Value does.

Grouping related properties into one typed, optionally validated class keeps them together, makes the relationship between them visible in one place, and can fail fast at startup on missing or invalid values in a way six scattered @Value fields don't provide by default.
@Value is being deprecated in favor of @ConfigurationProperties and will eventually stop working.
@Value can only inject String values, so numeric or boolean configuration requires @ConfigurationProperties.
assessments.explanation: One class documents the full shape of a related configuration group in one place instead of six independent injection points scattered across unrelated classes, and adding @Validated with constraint annotations gives a fail-fast startup check that six separate @Value fields have no equivalent for. The “@Value is being deprecated in favor…” option is false: @Value remains fully supported and is appropriate for standalone properties. The “@ConfigurationProperties resolves properties faster at runtime than @Value does” option is false: both resolve at startup, and reading a field afterward costs the same. The “@Value can only inject String values…” option is false: @Value can and does resolve to numeric, boolean, and other simply-convertible types, not just String.

assessments.prompt: A field is declared `@Value("${app.reports.cron-expression}")`, with no default value written into the placeholder at all. The property app.reports.cron-expression does not appear in any registered property source. What happens at application startup?
options: The field is silently left null, and the application starts normally.
The application starts successfully, and a NullPointerException is thrown the first time application code reads the field.
Spring automatically substitutes an empty string "" for the unresolved property.
Spring throws IllegalArgumentException: Could not resolve placeholder 'app.reports.cron-expression'.
assessments.explanation: A @Value placeholder with no colon-separated default has nothing to fall back on if the referenced property is missing everywhere: Spring does not inject null in that case, it throws IllegalArgumentException while resolving the placeholder, which fails the whole application startup immediately, before the bean is even fully constructed. This fail-fast behavior is why @Value is a reasonable choice for a required property with no sensible default. The “The field is silently left null…”, “Spring automatically substitutes an empty string ""…”, and “The application starts successfully, and a NullPointerException…” options all describe a silent or deferred failure, which a placeholder without a default does not allow.

assessments.prompt: A class is annotated `@ConfigurationProperties(prefix = "app.mail")` only -- no @Component, no @EnableConfigurationProperties on any @Configuration class, and it isn't covered by any @ConfigurationPropertiesScan. What happens to its fields at runtime?
options: The application fails to start, because @ConfigurationProperties always requires an explicit registration mechanism to be present.
Spring Boot automatically detects and binds any @ConfigurationProperties class found anywhere on the classpath, similar to how @Entity classes are discovered.
The class is never registered as a Spring bean at all, so nothing ever binds real configuration values onto it.
Spring falls back to binding its fields the same way @Value placeholders are resolved, without requiring bean registration.
assessments.explanation: @ConfigurationProperties is metadata describing a binding target's prefix and shape. It is not a stereotype annotation, and on its own it does nothing to make Spring register the class as a bean. Without @Component, @EnableConfigurationProperties, or @ConfigurationPropertiesScan making it a bean through some route, the class is never constructed by the container in a way that triggers binding, so any instance your own code creates keeps its Java-level defaults. The “Spring Boot automatically detects and binds any…” option invents an automatic discovery mechanism @ConfigurationProperties doesn't have on its own. The “The application fails to start, because @ConfigurationProperties…” option is wrong: startup fails only if some other bean tries to inject the class; an unregistered class nobody injects is ignored. The “Spring falls back to binding its fields…” option describes a fallback that doesn't exist.

assessments.prompt: A constructor-bound, @Validated @ConfigurationProperties class has a field annotated @Min(0) for retryCount. A deployment sets app.notifications.retry-count=-1. What happens when the application starts?
options: The application fails to start, because Spring Boot validates the fully-bound object against its declared constraints immediately after binding and refuses to start if any constraint fails.
The class binds successfully with retryCount set to -1; @Min(0) is documentation only, with no actual enforcement at binding time.
retryCount is silently clamped to the nearest valid value, 0, with no error or log message.
The @Min(0) constraint is only checked the first time application code actually reads retryCount, not during startup.
assessments.explanation: @Validated on a @ConfigurationProperties class triggers Bean Validation against the fully-bound object at application startup, using the same constraint annotations as request DTOs: a violated constraint stops startup, and Boot's failure report names the property, the rejected value and the constraint that failed. The “The class binds successfully with retryCount set…” and “retryCount is silently clamped to the nearest…” options are wrong because the constraint is enforced, and nothing is auto-corrected. The “The @Min(0) constraint is only checked…” option incorrectly defers validation to first use, when it runs once, eagerly, right after the object is bound at startup.

assessments.prompt: A developer defaults to @Value for every single configuration value, arguing it's simpler and requires less code than defining a whole @ConfigurationProperties class. Explain when that's a reasonable choice and when it starts to break down.
assessments.modelAnswer: For a single, standalone property that needs no validation beyond type conversion, @Value is the simpler choice: one annotation, no class to define or register. The tradeoffs start showing up once you have several RELATED properties scattered across @Value fields in different classes: there's no single place that documents 'these six properties all belong to configuring the email subsystem,' so understanding the full shape of that configuration means hunting across however many classes happen to inject pieces of it. It gets worse around missing or mistyped keys: a @Value field with a default falls back to that default whenever the property is typo'd or omitted, with no signal that anything is wrong. A grouped @ConfigurationProperties class fixes both problems at once: all six related properties live as fields on one class, under one prefix, and adding @Validated with constraint annotations turns a missing or invalid value into a startup failure. A grouped class also gives tests and tooling one typed object to read or construct, instead of six loose values. My rule: @Value for a few independent, simple properties; @ConfigurationProperties as soon as there is a group of related settings, or a misconfigured value would cause a production problem.

concepts.title: Spring Profiles and Externalized Configuration
concepts.description: Profiles let a single build artifact swap in different beans and property overlays per environment through @Profile and application-{profile}.properties, and externalizing configuration -- keeping secrets and environment-specific values out of the files you commit -- is what makes that same artifact safely deployable from local development through production without rebuilding it or leaking a credential into source control.
learningObjectives: Activate a Spring profile via spring.profiles.active and explain how application-{profile}.properties layers on top of, rather than replaces, application.properties.
Use @Profile on a @Bean or @Component to conditionally include or exclude it from the context depending on which profile is active.
Predict what happens when zero, one, or more than one @Profile-guarded bean of the same type is eligible under the currently active profiles.
Explain why hardcoding environment-specific values and secrets directly into application.properties and committing them to source control is a serious, hard-to-reverse mistake.
Explain the 'build once, promote everywhere' principle and how profiles combined with externalized configuration make one build artifact deployable across every environment without recompilation.
Predict the effect of activating two profiles simultaneously with overlapping properties or overlapping @Profile beans.

sections.heading: Activating Profiles and Layered Property Files
sections.body:
A **profile** is a named label (`dev`, `staging`, `prod`, or anything else you choose) that you activate at startup via the property `spring.profiles.active`, set through any of the sources from the precedence concept: a command-line argument (`--spring.profiles.active=prod`), an environment variable (`SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE=prod`, using the same relaxed-binding rules), or, less commonly for a value that's meant to vary per deployment, directly in `application.properties`.

Once a profile is active, Spring Boot looks for a file named `application-{profile}.properties` (or `.yml`), so `application-prod.properties` for `prod`, and, if it exists, loads it **in addition to** the base `application.properties`, not instead of it. Properties defined only in the base file remain in effect; properties defined in both files take the profile-specific file's value, because profile-specific files rank above the base file. This lets `application.properties` hold every setting that's the same everywhere, while `application-prod.properties` holds only the handful of values that differ for production (a connection pool size, a log level, a feature flag) without duplicating everything else. Because it is layering and not replacement, a profile file that omits a key never leaves the application without a value for it.

sections.heading: @Profile on Beans: Swapping Implementations by Environment
Multiple Active Profiles and Property Merging
sections.body:
`spring.profiles.active` can list more than one profile, comma-separated: `spring.profiles.active=prod,metrics`. Each active profile contributes its own `application-{profile}.properties` overlay, and where two active profiles' files define the same key, the later one in the list takes precedence over the earlier one, so order matters. This is useful for composing independent concerns (`prod` for the bulk of production settings, `metrics` for turning on a separate monitoring integration that isn't specific to any one environment) rather than needing a dedicated `prod-with-metrics` profile for every combination you might ever want.

It's also the mechanism behind the ambiguous-bean scenario from the previous section: if a deployment script activates `dev,prod` together (through a copy-paste mistake, a misconfigured CI variable, or forgetting that profiles compose) both `@Profile("dev")` and `@Profile("prod")` beans of the same type become simultaneously eligible, and Spring refuses to guess between them. Spring has no notion of mutually exclusive profiles and will not stop you from combining them; the ambiguity only surfaces at startup. Keep `dev`, `staging` and `prod` mutually exclusive in the deployment tooling, for example by having the pipeline set one profile variable per environment instead of anyone typing it by hand. If you do want one name to switch on several profiles, Boot supports profile groups, such as `spring.profiles.group.production=proddb,prodmq`.

sections.heading: Externalizing Configuration: Why Secrets Don't Belong in application.properties
sections.body:
Hardcoding a real database password or third-party API key directly into `application.properties` (or a profile-specific overlay) and committing it to source control is hard to undo, because git history keeps it: deleting the line in a later commit does not remove it from history, anyone with clone access (including CI systems, contractors, and, if the repository is ever made public or forked, a far wider audience than originally intended) can retrieve it from an earlier revision indefinitely, and rotating a leaked credential after the fact is disruptive compared to never having leaked it. It also breaks the 'build once, promote everywhere' principle covered next, since a file with production secrets baked in either has to be different from the file used in every other environment (forcing environment-specific builds again) or, worse, gives development and CI environments production credentials on checkout.

The fix: keep `application.properties` and any profile overlay free of actual secrets, referencing them only as a placeholder with **no default**, `spring.datasource.password=${DB_PASSWORD}`, and supply the value at deploy time from outside source control: an environment variable injected by the container platform, a secrets manager (Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, Kubernetes Secrets), or a dedicated configuration server. What happens when `DB_PASSWORD` is forgotten is less tidy than with `@Value`. `spring.datasource.*` is bound by `@ConfigurationProperties`, and that binder leaves an unresolvable placeholder as literal text, so the driver tries to log in with the password `${DB_PASSWORD}` and the database rejects it. With JPA you see that authentication error at startup; without anything that connects early, you see it on the first query. No wrong credential is accepted, but if you want a clear message, bind the secret in your own `@Validated` properties class or read it through `@Value`, which throws on an unresolved placeholder.

sections.heading: Build Once, Promote Everywhere
sections.body: Put together, profiles and externalized configuration are what let a team build exactly **one** artifact (one jar, one container image, never rebuilt for a different environment) and promote it through dev, staging, and production, with each environment supplying its own profile activation and its own externally-injected secrets and environment-specific values at the moment it runs. An artifact that's rebuilt separately per environment can subtly differ between the version that was tested in staging and the version that ships to production (a different dependency resolution, a different compiler flag, a different baked-in value), so staging tested something that only resembles what runs in production, which defeats the purpose of testing in staging. Building once and promoting the unchanged binary, with every environment difference supplied by profile activation and external configuration, closes that gap.

examples.title: Layered Base and Profile-Specific Property Files
examples.code:
# application.properties (base -- applies everywhere)
spring.datasource.url=jdbc:postgresql://localhost:5432/orders
spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto=none
app.notifications.channel=email

# application-prod.properties (overlay -- only when prod is active)
spring.datasource.url=jdbc:postgresql://prod-db.internal:5432/orders
spring.jpa.show-sql=false
examples.explanation: With spring.profiles.active=prod, spring.datasource.url resolves to the production overlay's value: the profile-specific file wins for any key both files define. spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto=none and app.notifications.channel=email, defined ONLY in the base file, remain fully in effect under the prod profile too, since application-prod.properties is loaded as an ADDITION to the base file, not a replacement; there is no need to repeat every base setting in the prod overlay just to keep it active. spring.jpa.show-sql=false, present only in the prod overlay, has no base-file counterpart; under other profiles the setting falls back to Spring Boot's own default, which is also false.

examples.title: Swapping a Bean Implementation With @Profile
examples.explanation: Any @Service depending on Notifier through its constructor never needs to know which of these two implementations it received. With dev active, component scanning registers only LoggingNotifier, so injection resolves to it unambiguously; with prod active, only SesNotifier. The swap depends only on which profile is active, with no change to any class that uses Notifier, and developers can run the app locally without sending email to customers.

examples.title: Externalizing a Database Password Instead of Hardcoding It
examples.code:
# application.properties -- committed to source control, contains NO real secret
spring.datasource.username=orders_app
spring.datasource.password=${DB_PASSWORD}

# Deployment: the container's environment supplies the real value
# DB_PASSWORD=<retrieved from a secrets manager at deploy time, never committed anywhere>
#
# If DB_PASSWORD is missing at startup, the binder leaves the literal text
# ${DB_PASSWORD} as the password and the database rejects the login, e.g.
# PostgreSQL: FATAL: password authentication failed for user "orders_app"
examples.explanation: The committed application.properties file contains a placeholder, ${DB_PASSWORD}, with no default value: the actual password never appears anywhere in the repository or its history, because no committed file contains it. At deploy time the Environment resolves the placeholder from an environment variable populated by a secrets manager. If the variable is missing, the login fails. The error talks about authentication rather than a missing variable, so when you see it, check that DB_PASSWORD reached the container before you start rotating passwords. (The message in the code comment is PostgreSQL's; other databases word it differently.)

misconceptions.description: application-prod.properties replaces application.properties entirely when the prod profile is active -- only the values in the profile-specific file are actually used.
misconceptions.clarification: Profile-specific files are loaded as a layered OVERLAY on top of the base application.properties, not a full replacement of it. Any key defined only in the base file remains fully in effect under any active profile; a profile-specific file only needs to define the handful of keys that differ for that environment. Only keys that are defined in BOTH files have their base-file value overridden by the profile-specific one: everything else in the base file is untouched and still applies.
misconceptions.fact: Profile-specific files are loaded as a layered OVERLAY on top of the base application.properties, not a full replacement of it.

misconceptions.description: It's fine to commit real production secrets into application.properties as long as the repository itself is private.
misconceptions.clarification: A private repository still typically grants access to CI/CD systems, every current team member and contractor, and often a build/audit trail that retains history indefinitely, and once a secret is committed, deleting the line in a later commit does not remove it from git history, where it remains retrievable by anyone who can access any earlier revision. 'Private' also doesn't protect against the repository later being made public, forked, or migrated, at which point a secret committed months or years earlier becomes exposed retroactively. Externalizing secrets through environment variables or a secrets manager, referenced only via a placeholder in the committed file, means the repository never contains one.

exercises.prompt: Given these two files and spring.profiles.active=prod, what are the final effective values of spring.jpa.show-sql, app.max-upload-mb, and app.support-email once the application starts?
exercises.code:
# application.properties
spring.jpa.show-sql=true
app.max-upload-mb=10
app.support-email=support@example.com

# application-prod.properties
spring.jpa.show-sql=false
app.max-upload-mb=25
hints: application-prod.properties is loaded IN ADDITION to application.properties, not as a full replacement of it -- which keys does it actually redefine here?
For any key defined in BOTH files, the profile-specific file's value wins. For a key defined in ONLY the base file, there's nothing to override it with.
app.support-email never appears in application-prod.properties at all -- what happens to a base-file value that the profile overlay simply doesn't mention?
exercises.expectedAnswer: spring.jpa.show-sql resolves to false (overridden by the prod file), app.max-upload-mb resolves to 25 (overridden by the prod file), and app.support-email resolves to support@example.com (defined only in the base file, and therefore untouched and still in effect, since the prod file never mentions it at all).
exercises.solutionExplanation: application-prod.properties is loaded as a layered overlay on top of application.properties, not a replacement, so every key present in the base file remains in effect unless the profile-specific file also defines that same key. spring.jpa.show-sql and app.max-upload-mb are both defined in application-prod.properties, so their profile-specific values (false and 25) take precedence over the base file's (true and 10). app.support-email has no entry anywhere in application-prod.properties at all, so there is nothing to override its base-file value, and it resolves to support@example.com whichever profile is active.

exercises.prompt: A CI pipeline's integration test step sets `spring.profiles.active=dev,prod` (a leftover from a copy-pasted deployment script) and the application now fails to start with NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException for the Notifier type. Given the beans below, explain the bug and fix the CI configuration.
hints: spring.profiles.active accepts a comma-separated list -- what does activating BOTH dev and prod at once do to which @Profile beans are eligible for injection?
LoggingNotifier and SesNotifier both implement Notifier -- if both of their guarding profiles are active simultaneously, are they both eligible for the same injection point at once?
The fix isn't in the Java code at all -- the two beans and their @Profile annotations are correct. Fix the CI environment variable so only ONE of dev or prod is active for this test run.
exercises.solutionCode:
# Corrected CI environment variable -- activate exactly one profile for this test run:
# SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE=dev
exercises.solutionExplanation: With SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE=dev,prod, both dev and prod are simultaneously active, which makes BOTH @Profile("dev") LoggingNotifier and @Profile("prod") SesNotifier eligible for registration at the same time. Both implement Notifier, and with no @Primary or @Qualifier to disambiguate between them, Spring cannot decide which one to inject wherever a Notifier is required, so it refuses to start the application with NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException, naming both conflicting beans. The Java code is correct as written; the two beans were meant as alternatives. The bug is the leftover CI configuration activating both profiles: correcting SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE to name only dev (the profile appropriate for an integration test run) resolves the ambiguity, since only LoggingNotifier's guarding profile is active at that point.

assessments.prompt: spring.profiles.active=staging is set, and both application.properties and application-staging.properties exist, each defining a value for app.log-level (among other keys). What best describes how the final configuration is assembled?
options: application-staging.properties completely replaces application.properties -- only its values are used at all.
Having the same key in both files causes a startup error, since profile-specific files must not duplicate base-file keys.
application-staging.properties is loaded as an overlay on top of application.properties; for app.log-level the staging file's value wins, but any key defined only in the base file remains in effect.
Spring Boot merges the two files by keeping whichever value appears first alphabetically by key.
assessments.explanation: Profile-specific files layer on top of the base application.properties rather than replacing it outright: keys defined only in the base file remain fully in effect, and for keys defined in both, the profile-specific file's value takes precedence because it ranks higher in Spring Boot's property source precedence order. The “application-staging.properties completely replaces application.properties -- only…” option is wrong because it describes full replacement, not layering. The “Spring Boot merges the two files…” option describes behavior Spring Boot does not implement. The “Having the same key in both files…” option is wrong: defining the same key in both a base and profile-specific file is how profile-specific overrides work.

assessments.prompt: Two beans implement Notifier: one annotated @Profile("dev"), the other @Profile("prod"). The application starts with spring.profiles.active=staging -- a third profile matching neither bean. What happens when something requires a Notifier bean?
options: The application fails to start with NoSuchBeanDefinitionException.
Both beans are registered anyway, since @Profile only affects startup log output, not actual bean registration.
Spring picks whichever bean happens to be declared first in the source code as a reasonable fallback.
Spring Boot automatically constructs a default, no-op Notifier implementation whenever no profile-guarded bean matches the active profile.
assessments.explanation: @Profile excludes a bean from registration when its guarding profile isn't active. With staging active, neither LoggingNotifier's dev guard nor SesNotifier's prod guard matches, so neither bean is registered, and the moment something needs a Notifier, Spring finds none available and fails startup with NoSuchBeanDefinitionException, the same unresolved-dependency failure you get from ordinary IoC with no profiles involved. The “Spring picks whichever bean happens…”, “Both beans are registered anyway, since @Profile…”, and “Spring Boot automatically constructs a default, no-op…” options each describe behavior Spring does not have.

assessments.prompt: spring.profiles.active=prod,metrics is set, and both application-prod.properties and application-metrics.properties define a value for management.endpoint.health.show-details, with different values. Which value wins?
options: The base application.properties's value, since Spring Boot discards both conflicting overlays and falls back to the base file.
application-metrics.properties's value, because when two active profiles' overlay files define the same key, the LATER profile listed in spring.profiles.active takes precedence over an earlier one.
application-prod.properties's value, because prod is listed first in spring.profiles.active.
Neither -- defining the same key across two simultaneously active profiles' files causes a startup error.
assessments.explanation: When two active profiles' files define the same key, the later profile in the list wins. Here, metrics is listed after prod, so application-metrics.properties's value for the shared key wins. Order is therefore a deliberate choice: list the more specific or more important overlay last. The “application-prod.properties's value, because prod is listed first in spring.profiles.active” option reverses this rule. The “Neither -- defining the same key across…” option invents a startup error that doesn't occur; overlapping keys across active profile files are resolved deterministically, not treated as a conflict. The “The base application.properties's value, since Spring Boot…” option is wrong: the winning overlay's value is used, not a fallback to the base file.

assessments.prompt: A team externalizes their database password using `spring.datasource.password=${DB_PASSWORD:changeme}` (with a default of 'changeme'), rather than `${DB_PASSWORD}` with no default at all. What risk does adding that default introduce?
options: Placeholder defaults are resolved at build time, so 'changeme' would already be permanently baked into the compiled artifact regardless of which environment it runs in.
The default value only applies during local development and is automatically stripped out whenever spring.profiles.active=prod is set.
The application will always fail to start, since placeholders in application.properties are not permitted to have defaults.

If DB_PASSWORD is ever missing at deploy time (a misconfigured container, a forgotten secret), the application uses the well-known fallback password 'changeme', and on any database that still accepts that password it connects and looks healthy instead of failing.
assessments.explanation: Without a default, a missing DB_PASSWORD leaves the unresolved text ${DB_PASSWORD} as the password and the login is rejected, so someone notices. With a default of 'changeme', a deployment that forgets the secret can connect to any database where that password was never changed, with a credential anyone who reads the repository knows, and nothing signals the mistake. The “The application will always fail to start…” option is false: placeholders can have defaults; that's the mechanism being misused here. The “The default value only applies during local…” option invents automatic, profile-aware default-stripping that doesn't exist. The “Placeholder defaults are resolved at build time…” option misunderstands property resolution as a build-time step; it happens at runtime, against the running Environment.

assessments.prompt: A team currently maintains three separately-built jars -- one per environment -- each with its own hardcoded database credentials baked into application.properties before every deployment. Explain, using profiles and externalized configuration, how to move to a single build artifact promoted across all three environments, and why that's a meaningfully better practice.
assessments.modelAnswer: The core problem with three separately-built jars is that the artifact tested in staging is never the artifact that reaches production: each environment gets its own build, with its own baked-in database credentials and environment-specific settings, so a difference introduced during any one of those three separate build steps (a dependency resolving slightly differently, a configuration value typo'd only in the production build) can diverge from what was verified in staging. Hardcoding real credentials into each build's application.properties compounds this: those secrets end up committed to source control (or baked into a build artifact) at least once per environment, where anyone with repository access can read them, private or not. The fix is to build exactly one artifact and promote that unchanged binary through dev, staging, and production, letting environment differences come from two mechanisms external to the build itself. First, Spring profiles: keep application.properties limited to settings that are the same everywhere, and let a small, non-secret application-{profile}.properties overlay per environment (dev, staging, prod) supply only the handful of settings that legitimately differ, activated at deploy time via spring.profiles.active rather than baked in at build time. Second, externalized configuration for anything sensitive or deployment-specific: rather than hardcoding a database password into any properties file, reference it as a placeholder with no default (spring.datasource.password=${DB_PASSWORD}) and supply the value through an environment variable or secrets manager at the moment each environment's container starts. The same jar then behaves correctly in each environment, no credentials sit in git, and rotating one means changing the secret and restarting, not rebuilding. Promotion then means the same image or jar that passed testing in staging is the one that runs in production, which is what makes the staging result worth trusting.
